phy_edx.4.0.summary: When light meets a boundary between two materials it can be **reflected** (bounce back), **refracted** (change direction as it changes speed) or, if conditions are right, **totally internally reflected**. The law of reflection says the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, refraction happens because light changes speed between materials, and total internal reflection happens only when light travels from a denser to a less dense medium at an angle of incidence greater than the **critical angle**. You must be able to explain all three with accurate ray diagrams, measuring every angle from the normal.

core.p: Every mark in this topic depends on drawing and reading ray diagrams correctly. A ray is a straight line with an arrow showing the direction light travels. All angles are measured between the ray and the **normal**, never between the ray and the surface.
bullets: Draw rays with a **ruler** and put an **arrow** on every ray showing direction of travel.
The **normal** is a construction line drawn at **90 degrees to the surface** at the point where the ray hits it; draw it **dashed**.
The **angle of incidence (i)** is between the incident ray and the normal.
The **angle of reflection (r)** or **angle of refraction (r)** is between the outgoing ray and the normal.
Use a **protractor** centred on the point where the ray meets the boundary to measure angles.
Label media (for example air, glass, water) on each side of a boundary.

callouts.p: A line drawn at right angles (90 degrees) to a surface at the point where a ray meets it.
If a question gives the angle between the ray and the surface, subtract it from 90 degrees to get the angle of incidence.

core.h: Reflection and the law of reflection
core.p: Reflection happens when a wave bounces off a boundary and stays in the same medium. Because the light does not change medium, its speed, wavelength and frequency do not change, only its direction does.
bullets: **Law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection** (i = r).
The incident ray, reflected ray and normal all lie in the **same plane**.
A ray hitting a mirror **along the normal** (i = 0) is reflected straight back along itself.
Smooth, shiny surfaces such as mirrors reflect light in a single direction, giving clear images.
Reflection happens at every boundary to some extent: when light refracts into glass, a **weak partial reflection** also occurs.

callouts.p: The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal.

fig.cap: Law of reflection at a plane mirror. The normal is drawn at 90 degrees to the mirror where the ray hits it; the angle of incidence i equals the angle of reflection r, both measured from the normal.

core.p: When you look in a flat (plane) mirror, reflected rays reach your eye and your brain traces them back in straight lines to a point behind the mirror. No light actually comes from behind the mirror, so the image is virtual.
bullets: The image is **virtual** (cannot be projected on a screen).
The image is **upright** and the **same size** as the object.
The image is the **same distance behind** the mirror as the object is in front.
The image is **laterally inverted** (left and right swapped).

core.p: Refraction is the change in direction of a wave when it crosses a boundary between two different materials at an angle. It happens because the wave changes **speed** as it enters the new medium.
bullets: Light entering a **denser** medium (for example air to glass) **slows down** and bends **towards the normal**: angle of refraction is smaller than angle of incidence.
Light entering a **less dense** medium (for example glass to air) **speeds up** and bends **away from the normal**: angle of refraction is larger than angle of incidence.
A ray travelling **along the normal** (i = 0) does **not change direction**, but it still changes speed.
The **frequency does not change** when light refracts (it is set by the source).
Since wave speed = frequency x wavelength, when the speed falls the **wavelength decreases**, and when the speed rises the wavelength increases.
Here 'denser' means **optically denser**: a material in which light travels more slowly.

callouts.p: The change in direction of a wave as it passes from one medium into another, caused by a change in the speed of the wave.
Students often say frequency changes. It does not: only speed and wavelength change on refraction.

core.h: Why light refracts: the wavefront explanation
core.p: Think of a wavefront (a line joining the crests of the wave) reaching a glass block at an angle. One end of the wavefront reaches the glass first and slows down, while the other end is still in air travelling fast. The fast end catches up less, so the wavefront swings round and changes direction.
bullets: The part of the wavefront that enters the denser medium first **slows first**.
The rest of the wavefront is still moving faster, so the wavefront **pivots** towards the normal.
If the wave hits the boundary **along the normal**, the whole wavefront slows **at the same time**, so there is no change of direction.
Wavefronts are **closer together** in the denser medium because the wavelength is shorter.

callouts.p: Say 'the light changes speed' and 'one side of the wavefront slows down first'. Just saying 'the light bends' gets no explanation mark.

core.h: Refraction through a rectangular glass block
core.p: A ray passing through a parallel sided glass block refracts twice: towards the normal on entry and away from the normal on exit. Because the two faces are parallel, the emerging ray is parallel to the incident ray but shifted sideways.
bullets: At the first face (air to glass): slows down, bends **towards** the normal.
At the second face (glass to air): speeds up, bends **away from** the normal.
The emergent ray is **parallel** to the incident ray but **laterally displaced** (shifted sideways).
The angle of refraction inside the glass at entry equals the angle of incidence at the exit face (alternate angles).

callouts.p: For a rectangular block the ray leaves travelling in the same direction it entered, just shifted sideways.

core.p: When light travels from a denser medium towards a less dense one, it bends away from the normal. As the angle of incidence increases, the refracted ray gets closer and closer to the boundary. Beyond a certain angle no light can leave at all, and all of it is reflected back inside.
bullets: Condition 1: light must travel from a **denser medium to a less dense medium** (for example glass to air, water to air).
Condition 2: the **angle of incidence must be greater than the critical angle**.
In TIR **all** the light is reflected; none is refracted out, so the reflected ray is **bright** (no energy lost to a refracted ray).
TIR obeys the **law of reflection**: angle of incidence = angle of reflection.
TIR **cannot** happen when light goes from air into glass, because the light bends towards the normal and can always enter.

callouts.p: The complete reflection of light at a boundary when it travels from a denser medium to a less dense medium with an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle.
In 'state the conditions' questions you must give BOTH: denser to less dense, AND angle of incidence greater than the critical angle.

core.p: The critical angle is the angle of incidence that is the dividing line between light escaping by refraction and light being totally internally reflected. At exactly the critical angle the refracted ray travels along the boundary.
bullets: **Below** the critical angle (i less than c): most light **refracts out** away from the normal; a weak partial reflection also occurs.
**At** the critical angle (i = c): the angle of refraction is **90 degrees**; the refracted ray travels **along the boundary**.
**Above** the critical angle (i greater than c): **total internal reflection**.
The critical angle depends on the material: approximately **42 degrees for glass**, about **49 degrees for water**, about **24 degrees for diamond**.
The more light slows down in a material, the **smaller** its critical angle, so TIR happens more easily.

callouts.p: The angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the angle of refraction is 90 degrees.

fig.cap: Light inside glass meeting a glass to air boundary at three angles of incidence. Left: i is less than the critical angle so the ray refracts out (with weak reflection). Middle: at the critical angle the refracted ray runs along the boundary. Right: above the critical angle all the light is totally internally reflected.

core.p: A common class experiment uses a ray box and a semicircular glass (or acrylic) block. The ray is aimed at the centre of the flat face through the curved side, so it enters the curved surface along a normal and does not bend there; only the flat face refracts it.
bullets: Aim the ray through the **curved face towards the centre** of the flat face so it meets the curved face along the normal (no refraction there).
Slowly increase the angle of incidence at the flat face and watch the emerging ray bend further from the normal.
Record the angle of incidence when the emerging ray just travels **along the flat face**: this is the **critical angle**.
Increase the angle further and observe **total internal reflection**: the reflected ray becomes bright.
Use a **narrow ray**, a darkened room and a sharp pencil to mark rays, and measure with a protractor from the normal to reduce uncertainty.

callouts.p: The curved face means the ray always travels along a radius, which is a normal to the curved surface, so it enters undeviated and only one refraction needs to be considered.

core.h: Uses of total internal reflection: optical fibres
core.p: An optical fibre is a very thin, flexible strand of glass or plastic. Light enters one end and repeatedly hits the inside wall at angles greater than the critical angle, so it is totally internally reflected again and again and travels along the fibre, even round gentle bends.
bullets: Each reflection is **total**, so very little light energy is lost and signals travel long distances.
Fibres have a dense **core** surrounded by a less dense **cladding**, so TIR happens at the core to cladding boundary and the cladding protects the surface.
**Communications**: fibres carry telephone, internet and TV signals as pulses of light (or infrared).
**Endoscopes**: bundles of fibres carry light into the body and an image back out, letting doctors see inside without major surgery.
If the fibre is bent too sharply, the angle of incidence can drop below the critical angle and light **escapes** by refraction.

callouts.p: Light hits the inside surface at an angle greater than the critical angle, so it is totally internally reflected repeatedly along the fibre.

fig.cap: An optical fibre. Light in the dense core strikes the core to cladding boundary at angles greater than the critical angle and is totally internally reflected each time, so it zigzags along the fibre with very little loss.

core.h: Other uses of total internal reflection
core.p: Glass prisms with 45 degree angles use TIR as a better mirror. Light enters a face along the normal, hits the long face at 45 degrees, which is greater than the critical angle of glass (about 42 degrees), and is totally reflected through 90 degrees or 180 degrees.
bullets: **Prismatic periscopes** and **binoculars**: two 45 degree prisms turn light through 90 degrees each; TIR gives a brighter, sharper image than a silvered mirror, which absorbs some light and can tarnish.
**Bicycle reflectors and cat's eyes**: prisms turn light back through 180 degrees towards the driver.
**Diamonds sparkle** because their very small critical angle (about 24 degrees) traps light by many total internal reflections before it escapes.
45 degrees works in glass only because it is **greater than** the critical angle of about 42 degrees.

callouts.p: Mark schemes reward 'TIR reflects all of the light' and 'mirrors absorb some light' when comparing prisms with mirrors.

core.p: At any boundary light can be reflected, refracted or both. Which dominates depends on the direction of travel (into a denser or less dense medium) and the angle of incidence. Seeing these as one connected picture is what grade 9 answers show.
bullets: **Reflection**: same medium, angle in = angle out, speed unchanged.
**Refraction**: new medium, speed changes, direction changes unless along the normal.
**Partial reflection** accompanies refraction: some light is always reflected at a boundary.
**TIR**: the special case where refraction becomes impossible, so all light is reflected.
All three are explained by **ray diagrams** with angles measured from the normal.

analogy.t: A marching band walking onto mud
analogy.p: Imagine a line of marchers walking at an angle from smooth tarmac onto thick mud. The marchers who reach the mud first slow down while the others are still on tarmac moving fast, so the whole line swings round and changes direction, just like a wavefront bending towards the normal. Walking from mud back onto tarmac, the first marchers speed up and the line swings away from the normal. If the line meets the edge at too shallow an angle when leaving the mud, it cannot get out and turns back, like total internal reflection. Where it breaks down: marchers are separate people who could choose to keep walking straight, and real light is a wave whose frequency stays fixed; also nothing in the analogy explains the weak partial reflection that always occurs at a real boundary.

terms.d: A straight line with an arrow showing the path and direction of travel of light.
A line at 90 degrees to a surface at the point where a ray meets it.
The angle between the incident ray and the normal.
The angle between the reflected ray and the normal.
The angle between the refracted ray and the normal.
The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
A wave bouncing off a boundary and staying in the same medium.
The change in direction of a wave as it crosses a boundary into a different medium, caused by a change in speed.
A medium in which light travels more slowly.
A line joining points on a wave that are in step, such as all the crests.
The weak reflection that occurs at a boundary when most of the light is refracted.
The angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the angle of refraction is 90 degrees.
Complete reflection of light inside a denser medium when it meets a boundary with a less dense medium at an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle.
A thin flexible glass or plastic strand that carries light along it by repeated total internal reflection.
A medical instrument using bundles of optical fibres to see inside the body.
The sideways shift of a ray that has passed through a parallel sided block.
An image that light rays only appear to come from, which cannot be projected on a screen.

mistakes.w: Measuring angles between the ray and the surface.
mistakes.r: All angles are measured between the ray and the normal.

mistakes.w: Light bends because it enters a different material.
mistakes.r: Light refracts because it changes speed as it enters a different medium.

mistakes.w: Frequency changes when light enters glass.
mistakes.r: Frequency stays the same; speed and wavelength decrease.

mistakes.w: Light going into glass bends away from the normal.
mistakes.r: Light slows down entering glass and bends towards the normal.

mistakes.w: TIR happens when the angle is big.
mistakes.r: TIR needs light travelling from a denser to a less dense medium AND an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle.

mistakes.w: The critical angle is when light is totally internally reflected.
mistakes.r: The critical angle is the angle of incidence for which the angle of refraction is 90 degrees.

mistakes.w: A ray along the normal is not refracted, so its speed does not change.
mistakes.r: It does not change direction, but its speed still changes.

mistakes.w: Optical fibres work by reflecting off a mirror coating.
mistakes.r: Light is totally internally reflected at the core boundary because the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle.

mistakes.w: Drawing rays without arrows or the normal as a solid line.
mistakes.r: Rays need arrows showing direction; the normal is a dashed line at 90 degrees to the surface.

exam.q: State the law of reflection.
model: Angle of incidence = angle of reflection (both measured from the normal).
exam.tip: Use the words incidence and reflection, not 'the angles are the same'.

exam.q: Define the critical angle.
model: The angle of incidence (in the denser medium)
for which the angle of refraction is 90 degrees.
exam.tip: Two parts: what the angle is and the 90 degree refraction condition.

exam.q: A ray of light strikes a plane mirror. The angle between the ray and the mirror surface is 25 degrees. Calculate the angle of reflection.
model: Angle of incidence = 90 - 25 = 65 degrees
Angle of reflection = 65 degrees
exam.tip: Always convert surface angles to angles from the normal first.

exam.q: Explain why a ray of light bends towards the normal when it passes from air into glass.
model: Light slows down in glass
one side of the wavefront enters and slows first, so the wavefront changes direction towards the normal
exam.tip: The key word is speed; mention the wavefront for the second mark.

exam.q: State two conditions needed for total internal reflection.
model: Light travelling from a denser medium to a less dense medium (for example glass to air)
Angle of incidence greater than the critical angle
exam.tip: 'Big angle' is not enough: say greater than the critical angle.

exam.q: A ray of light passes along the normal from air into a glass block. Describe what happens to its direction, speed and wavelength.
model: Direction does not change
Speed decreases
Wavelength decreases (frequency unchanged)
exam.tip: No change of direction does not mean nothing happens.

exam.q: Draw a ray diagram to show a ray of light passing through a rectangular glass block at an angle. Label the normals and describe the ray's path.
model: Normals drawn at 90 degrees to both faces at the points of entry and exit
Ray bends towards the normal on entering the glass
Ray bends away from the normal on leaving the glass
Emergent ray parallel to incident ray (laterally displaced)
exam.tip: Use a ruler, arrows on rays and dashed normals.

exam.q: Light in a glass block hits the glass to air boundary. The critical angle of the glass is 42 degrees. Describe what happens when the angle of incidence is 30 degrees, 42 degrees and 50 degrees.
model: 30 degrees: light refracts out away from the normal (with some weak reflection)
42 degrees: refracted ray travels along the boundary (angle of refraction 90 degrees)
50 degrees: total internal reflection, all light reflected at 50 degrees
exam.tip: Compare each angle with the critical angle.

exam.q: Explain why total internal reflection cannot happen when light travels from air into water.
model: Light slows down entering water so bends towards the normal
the angle of refraction is always less than 90 degrees so light can always enter / TIR needs denser to less dense
exam.tip: Link to the direction of bending.

exam.q: Explain how an optical fibre is able to carry light along its length, even when the fibre is curved.
model: Light enters the fibre (core)
Light hits the inner surface at an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle
Light is totally internally reflected
This happens repeatedly along the fibre so light travels along it with little loss (unless bent too sharply)
exam.tip: Key phrases: greater than the critical angle, totally internally reflected, repeatedly.

exam.q: Describe how you could use a ray box and a semicircular glass block to find the critical angle of glass and show total internal reflection.
model: Place the block on paper and draw round it; mark the centre of the flat face
Shine a narrow ray through the curved face towards the centre of the flat face so it enters along a normal
Draw the normal at the centre of the flat face
Increase the angle of incidence until the emergent ray travels along the flat face
Mark the ray and measure the angle of incidence from the normal with a protractor: this is the critical angle
Increase the angle further and observe total internal reflection; repeat and average; darken the room for a clear ray
exam.tip: Six mark answers need a logical sequence: setup, procedure, measurement, observation, improving reliability.

exam.q: Explain why prisms rather than plane mirrors are used in high quality periscopes.
model: Light hits the long face at 45 degrees, greater than the critical angle of glass (about 42 degrees)
so total internal reflection occurs and all the light is reflected
mirrors absorb some light / can tarnish, giving a dimmer image, so prisms give a brighter, clearer image
exam.tip: Quote the 45 degree versus 42 degree comparison.

worked.q: A ray of light hits a plane mirror. The angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray is 110 degrees. Find the angle of incidence and the angle between the reflected ray and the mirror.
steps: The normal bisects the angle between incident and reflected rays because i = r.
Angle of incidence = 110 / 2 = 55 degrees.
Angle of reflection = 55 degrees (law of reflection).
Angle between reflected ray and mirror = 90 - 55 = 35 degrees.
worked.ans: i = 55 degrees; reflected ray makes 35 degrees with the mirror surface.

worked.q: The critical angle of water is 49 degrees. A diver shines a torch upward towards the water surface. At what angles of incidence will the light (a) escape into the air, (b) be totally internally reflected? Explain.
steps: Light is travelling from water (denser) to air (less dense), so TIR is possible.
If the angle of incidence is less than 49 degrees, the angle of refraction is less than 90 degrees, so the light refracts out away from the normal.
At exactly 49 degrees the refracted ray travels along the water surface.
If the angle of incidence is greater than 49 degrees, all the light is totally internally reflected back into the water, with angle of reflection equal to the angle of incidence.
worked.ans: (a) Angles of incidence less than 49 degrees; (b) angles of incidence greater than 49 degrees.

worked.q: A ray enters the short face of a right angled 45 degree glass prism along the normal. The critical angle of the glass is 42 degrees. Describe and explain the path of the ray.
steps: At the first face the ray travels along the normal, so it slows down but does not change direction.
It meets the long (hypotenuse) face with an angle of incidence of 45 degrees.
45 degrees is greater than the critical angle of 42 degrees, and the ray is going from glass to air, so it is totally internally reflected.
Angle of reflection = 45 degrees, so the ray is turned through 90 degrees.
It meets the other short face along the normal and leaves without changing direction.
worked.ans: The ray is totally internally reflected at the long face and turned through 90 degrees, leaving the prism along the normal of the second short face.

phy_edx.4.1.summary: Whether a surface gives a clear image depends on how smooth it is: smooth surfaces give **specular reflection** in a single direction, while rough surfaces give **diffuse reflection**, scattering light in many directions. The colour we see depends on which wavelengths of light are **reflected, transmitted or absorbed**: an opaque object looks the colour it reflects, and a filter only transmits its own colour and absorbs the rest. Grade 9 answers link every colour effect back to differential absorption of wavelengths and explain diffuse reflection using the normal at each point of a rough surface.

core.h: Reflection recap: the law still applies
core.p: Both specular and diffuse reflection obey the law of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection at every point, measured from the normal. The difference between them comes entirely from the shape of the surface, which decides which way the normal points at each spot.
bullets: **Law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection**, at every point on any surface.
The **normal** is at 90 degrees to the surface at the point where the ray hits.
On a smooth surface all the normals are **parallel**.
On a rough surface the normals point in **many different directions**.
So the surface texture, not a failure of the law, decides whether reflection is specular or diffuse.

callouts.t: Diffuse does not break the law
callouts.p: Never write that diffuse reflection does not obey the law of reflection. It does, at every point; the normals just point different ways.

core.p: Specular reflection is reflection from a smooth surface in a single direction. Parallel rays arriving at a smooth surface all meet normals that point the same way, so they all reflect at the same angle and leave still parallel. This keeps the pattern of light from the object, so you see a clear image.
bullets: Happens at **smooth, shiny** surfaces: plane mirrors, polished metal, still water, glass.
Parallel incident rays are reflected as **parallel rays** in a **single direction**.
Produces a **clear (sharp) image**, which is why mirrors work.
The surface bumps are **much smaller than the wavelength** of light, so the surface acts as smooth.

callouts.p: Reflection from a smooth surface in a single direction.

core.p: Diffuse reflection is reflection from a rough surface, causing scattering. Each ray hits a part of the surface tilted a different way, so its normal points in a different direction; each ray obeys i = r about its own normal and therefore leaves in a different direction. The light is scattered, so no clear image forms.
bullets: Happens at **rough** surfaces: paper, painted walls, cloth, rough water.
Parallel incident rays are reflected in **many different directions** (scattered).
**No clear image** is formed, but the surface can be seen from any angle.
Most objects are seen by diffuse reflection: light scatters from them into our eyes from every direction.
A lake looks like a mirror when **still** (specular) but gives no clear reflection when **choppy** (diffuse).

callouts.p: Reflection from a rough surface causing scattering.

core.h: White light and the visible spectrum
core.p: White light is not a single colour. It is a mixture of all the colours of the visible spectrum, each with its own range of wavelengths and frequencies. Our eyes and brain detect which wavelengths arrive and we perceive this as colour.
bullets: Visible spectrum order: **red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet**.
**Red** has the **longest wavelength** and **lowest frequency** of visible light (about 700 nm).
**Violet** has the **shortest wavelength** and **highest frequency** of visible light (about 400 nm).
Each colour is a **range** of wavelengths; the spectrum is continuous.
A prism splits white light into this spectrum because each colour refracts by a slightly different amount.

callouts.p: The colour of light is decided by its wavelength (or frequency). Different colours are different wavelengths of visible light.

core.p: When light hits an object, each wavelength can be reflected (bounce off), transmitted (pass through) or absorbed (energy taken in by the material, usually warming it). Most materials treat different wavelengths differently, and this **differential absorption** is what creates colour.
bullets: **Reflected**: light bounces off the surface and can reach our eyes.
**Transmitted**: light passes through the material.
**Absorbed**: the light's energy is transferred to the material and the light is not seen.
**Opaque** objects transmit no light: they only reflect or absorb.
**Transparent** objects transmit light without scattering, so you can see clearly through them.
**Translucent** objects transmit light but scatter it, so you cannot see clearly through them (for example frosted glass).

callouts.p: Different wavelengths (colours) of light are absorbed by different amounts at a surface.

core.p: An opaque object looks the colour of the wavelengths it reflects. In white light a red object reflects red wavelengths and absorbs all the other colours, so only red light reaches your eye from it.
bullets: A **red** object **reflects red** light and **absorbs** all other colours.
A **green** object reflects green and absorbs the rest; similarly for any colour.
A **white** object **reflects all** wavelengths of visible light equally.
A **black** object **absorbs all** wavelengths of visible light and reflects none.
We see colour because the **reflected** wavelengths enter our eyes; the absorbed ones never do.
Black objects warm up fastest in sunlight because they absorb all the visible light energy.

callouts.p: An opaque object appears the colour of the light it reflects. White reflects all colours; black absorbs all colours.

core.p: What colour an object looks depends on both the object and the light shining on it. If the light does not contain the colour the object reflects, there is nothing for it to reflect, so it looks black.
bullets: Red object in **red light**: reflects the red, looks **red**.
Red object in **blue light**: absorbs blue, reflects nothing, looks **black**.
White object in **red light**: reflects all colours present, which is only red, so looks **red**.
White object in **green light**: looks **green**.
Black object in **any** light: looks **black**.
This is why clothes can look a different colour under coloured stage or street lighting.

callouts.p: Step 1: what colours are in the light arriving? Step 2: which of those does the object reflect? Only those are seen; if none, it looks black.

core.p: A colour filter is a transparent coloured material that transmits only its own colour (range of wavelengths) and absorbs all the others. A red filter therefore turns white light into red light, not by adding red, but by removing every other colour.
bullets: A **red filter transmits red** and **absorbs** all other colours.
A **blue filter transmits blue** and absorbs the rest, and so on.
Filters **only remove** light; they never add or change colours.
Light through a filter is **dimmer** than the white light that went in, because energy has been absorbed.
Two different filters in a row (for example red then green) let **no light** through: red absorbs green, then green absorbs red.
Two of the **same** filters in a row transmit that colour (a little dimmer).

callouts.p: A filter that transmits only certain wavelengths (its own colour) and absorbs all other wavelengths.
Do not write that a filter 'turns the light red'. Say it absorbs all colours except red and transmits red.

core.p: Looking at an object through a filter combines both ideas. The object first decides which colours it reflects; then the filter decides which of those reach your eye.
bullets: Red object through a **red filter** (white light): red reflected, red transmitted, looks **red**.
Red object through a **green filter**: red reflected but absorbed by the filter, looks **black**.
White object through a **blue filter**: all colours reflected, only blue transmitted, looks **blue**.
Work in order: **light source, then object, then filter, then eye**.

callouts.p: Trace the light from the source to the eye, removing colours at each stage. Whatever survives is what you see; nothing surviving means black.

core.p: Coloured glass, coloured plastic and coloured liquids behave like filters. They transmit their own colour and absorb the others, so a stained glass window looks the colour of the light it lets through.
bullets: A **transparent coloured** object appears the colour it **transmits**.
An **opaque** object appears the colour it **reflects**.
Clear (colourless) glass transmits all visible wavelengths, so white light passes through as white.
Some objects both reflect and transmit some light, but at GCSE treat filters as transmitting and opaque objects as reflecting.

callouts.p: Opaque objects: colour = what is reflected. Transparent or translucent coloured objects: colour = what is transmitted.

core.p: Light is a wave that transfers energy. When a surface absorbs certain wavelengths, that energy is transferred to the material, usually increasing its thermal energy store. This connects colour to temperature effects.
bullets: Absorbed light energy increases the **thermal energy store** of the object.
**Black** surfaces absorb all visible wavelengths, so they heat up most in sunlight.
**White** surfaces reflect most light, so they stay cooler; this is why houses in hot countries are often painted white.
Filters warm up slightly because they absorb the colours they do not transmit.

core.h: Explaining colour like a grade 9 student
core.p: Top answers always explain colour using wavelengths and the three possible outcomes for light: reflected, transmitted or absorbed. They also say explicitly what happens to the colours that are not seen.
bullets: Name the colours **present** in the incoming light.
State which wavelengths are **reflected or transmitted** and which are **absorbed**.
Say which light **enters the eye** and hence the colour seen.
Use the phrase **'absorbs all other colours/wavelengths'**, which mark schemes credit.
For surfaces, link **smooth to specular to clear image** and **rough to diffuse to scattering**.

callouts.p: Many students only say what is reflected. Full marks usually need what is absorbed as well.

analogy.t: A nightclub bouncer with a guest list
analogy.p: Think of a red filter as a bouncer whose guest list says only 'red'. A crowd of all the colours (white light) arrives at the door: red gets in (transmitted) and everyone else is turned away and absorbed. A second bouncer whose list says only 'green' turns away the red guest, so nobody gets through two different filters. An opaque red object is like a bouncer who sends red back out the way it came (reflected) and keeps the rest. Where it breaks down: a real filter does not choose; it absorbs wavelengths because of how its material interacts with light, the absorbed energy heats the filter, and real filters pass a range of wavelengths and are never perfect, so some light of nearby colours can leak through.

terms.d: Reflection from a smooth surface in a single direction.
Reflection from a rough surface causing scattering.
The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal.
A line at 90 degrees to a surface at the point where light meets it.
Light being sent off in many different directions.
A mixture of all the colours (wavelengths) of the visible spectrum.
The continuous range of wavelengths of light that the eye can detect, from red (longest) to violet (shortest).
The distance from one point on a wave to the same point on the next wave; for light it decides the colour.
Light that bounces off a surface.
Light that passes through a material.
Light whose energy is taken in by a material, so it is not reflected or transmitted.
Different wavelengths of light being absorbed by different amounts at a surface.
Does not transmit any light.
Transmits light without scattering, so objects can be seen clearly through it.
Transmits light but scatters it, so objects cannot be seen clearly through it.
A material that transmits only certain wavelengths (its own colour) and absorbs all others.

mistakes.w: Diffuse reflection does not obey the law of reflection.
mistakes.r: Each ray obeys i = r, but the normals point in different directions on a rough surface, so rays scatter.

mistakes.w: A red filter turns white light red.
mistakes.r: A red filter transmits red light and absorbs all other colours.

mistakes.w: A red object absorbs red light.
mistakes.r: A red object reflects red light and absorbs all other colours.

mistakes.w: A black object reflects black light.
mistakes.r: A black object absorbs all colours (wavelengths) and reflects none.

mistakes.w: A red object in blue light looks purple or blue.
mistakes.r: It absorbs the blue and has no red light to reflect, so it looks black.

mistakes.w: Specular reflection happens on rough surfaces because the light 'spreads'.
mistakes.r: Specular reflection is from a smooth surface in a single direction; rough surfaces give diffuse reflection.

mistakes.w: White light is a colour on its own.
mistakes.r: White light is a mixture of all colours (wavelengths) of the visible spectrum.

mistakes.w: You can see an object because light comes out of it.
mistakes.r: Non-luminous objects are seen because light reflected (usually diffusely) from them enters the eye.

mistakes.w: Light through a red then a green filter looks yellow or brown.
mistakes.r: No light passes: the red filter absorbs green and the green filter absorbs red.

exam.q: State what is meant by specular reflection.
model: Reflection from a smooth surface in a single direction.
exam.tip: Mention both smooth and single direction.

exam.q: State what is meant by diffuse reflection.
model: Reflection from a rough surface causing scattering.
exam.tip: Rough and scattering are the key words.

exam.q: A student looks at a still lake and then the same lake on a windy day. Explain why she can see a clear reflection of the trees only on the still day.
model: Still water is a smooth surface, giving specular reflection
Parallel rays reflected in a single direction so the image is clear
Windy day: water surface is rough so reflection is diffuse
Light is scattered in many directions (normals point different ways) so no clear image
exam.tip: Contrast smooth and rough, and link each to the type of reflection and image.

exam.q: Explain why a sheet of white paper does not act as a mirror even though it reflects most of the light falling on it.
model: The paper surface is rough
so light is diffusely reflected / scattered in many directions, so no clear image forms
exam.tip: A surface can reflect a lot of light and still give no image.

exam.q: Explain why a green leaf looks green in white light.
model: The leaf reflects green light (wavelengths)
and absorbs all other colours
exam.tip: Say what happens to the other colours too.

exam.q: A red T-shirt is viewed in blue light. State and explain what colour it appears.
model: Black
The shirt absorbs blue light
There is no red light to reflect so no light reaches the eye from it
exam.tip: Coloured light questions: first list what light is available.

exam.q: White light passes through a blue filter. Describe what happens to the light.
model: Blue light is transmitted
All other colours are absorbed (light emerging is dimmer)
exam.tip: Transmitted and absorbed are the mark scheme words.

exam.q: White light passes through a red filter and then a green filter. Explain what is seen on a screen beyond the filters.
model: Red filter transmits only red and absorbs other colours
Green filter absorbs red light
So no light reaches the screen; it appears dark / black
exam.tip: Take the light through each filter in turn.

exam.q: Explain the difference between a transparent and a translucent material.
model: Transparent: transmits light without scattering so objects can be seen clearly through it
Translucent: transmits light but scatters it so objects cannot be seen clearly
exam.tip: Both transmit light; the difference is scattering.

exam.q: Explain how the colour of an object depends on the light falling on it and on the surface of the object. Use examples in your answer.
model: White light is a mixture of all colours / wavelengths
Opaque objects reflect some wavelengths and absorb others (differential absorption)
The colour seen is the colour of light reflected into the eye, e.g. a red object reflects red and absorbs others
White objects reflect all colours; black objects absorb all colours
In coloured light an object can only reflect colours that are present, e.g. red object in blue light looks black
A white object in red light looks red; filters transmit only their own colour and absorb the rest
exam.tip: Build up from white light, to opaque objects, to coloured light; give examples at each stage.

exam.q: Use the law of reflection to explain why a rough surface scatters light.
model: Each ray obeys the law of reflection (angle of incidence = angle of reflection)
On a rough surface the normals at different points point in different directions
So parallel incident rays are reflected in different directions (scattered)
exam.tip: The normal is the key idea; grade 9 answers mention it explicitly.

worked.q: A white ball, a red ball and a blue ball are placed under a red light in a dark room. What colour does each appear?
steps: Light available: only red.
White ball reflects all colours present, which is only red, so it looks red.
Red ball reflects red, so it looks red.
Blue ball reflects only blue, but there is no blue; it absorbs the red, so no light reflects and it looks black.
worked.ans: White ball: red. Red ball: red. Blue ball: black.

worked.q: A student views a white flower with a red centre through a red filter, in white light. What does she see?
steps: White petals reflect all colours of the white light.
The red filter transmits only the red part of that reflected light, so petals look red.
The red centre reflects red light only; the red filter transmits it, so the centre looks red.
Both parts look red, so the centre is hard to tell apart from the petals.
worked.ans: The whole flower looks red; the red centre no longer stands out.

worked.q: A green filter is placed over a torch and shone on a green apple and then on a red apple. Explain the colour of each apple.
steps: The green filter transmits only green light and absorbs other colours, so only green light reaches the apples.
Green apple reflects green light, so green light enters the eye: it looks green.
Red apple reflects only red; it absorbs the green and has nothing to reflect, so it looks black.
worked.ans: Green apple appears green; red apple appears black.

phy_edx.4.2.summary: Lenses work by **refraction**: a **converging** (convex) lens brings parallel rays together at a real principal focus, while a **diverging** (concave) lens spreads parallel rays out so they appear to come from a virtual principal focus. The more curved a lens is, the more it refracts light, so the **shorter its focal length** and the **more powerful** it is. Using ray diagrams you must show how converging lenses can form real or virtual images depending on where the object is, and how diverging lenses always form virtual, upright, diminished images.

core.p: A lens is a shaped piece of transparent material, usually glass or plastic, that changes the direction of light by refraction. Light slows down as it enters the lens and speeds up as it leaves, bending at both surfaces. The curved shape means rays hitting different parts of the lens bend by different amounts.
bullets: Lenses work by **refraction** at both surfaces.
A **converging lens** (convex) is **thicker in the middle** than at the edges.
A **diverging lens** (concave) is **thinner in the middle** than at the edges.
Rays hitting the lens further from the centre are bent **more**; a ray through the centre passes **straight through**.
In ray diagrams a lens is often drawn as a vertical line: arrowheads pointing **outwards** at the ends for converging, pointing **inwards** for diverging.

head: Lens
Shape
Effect on parallel rays
Focus
rows: Brings them together at a point
Virtual principal focus (rays appear to come from it)

callouts.p: Lenses change the direction of light by refraction, because light changes speed entering and leaving the lens material.

core.p: Ray diagram questions use a fixed set of terms, and mark schemes expect you to use them precisely. Learn these as definitions.
bullets: **Principal axis**: the horizontal line passing through the centre of the lens at 90 degrees to it.
**Optical centre**: the centre of the lens; rays through it pass straight through undeviated.
**Principal focus (F)**: the point where rays parallel to the principal axis meet after a converging lens, or appear to come from after a diverging lens.
**Focal length (f)**: the distance from the centre of the lens to the principal focus.
A lens has a principal focus on **each side**, at the same distance from the centre.
**2F** is the point at twice the focal length from the lens, a useful marker in ray diagrams.

callouts.p: The distance from the centre of the lens to the principal focus.
The point at which rays parallel to the principal axis are brought together (converging lens) or appear to come from (diverging lens).

core.p: When rays parallel to the principal axis pass through a converging lens, they are all refracted towards the axis and meet at the principal focus on the far side. Because the light actually passes through this point, it is a real focus, and a screen placed there would show a bright spot.
bullets: Parallel rays are **brought together (converge)** at the principal focus.
The ray along the principal axis passes straight through.
Rays further from the axis are bent **more**, so they all meet at the same point.
The focus is **real**: light really passes through it.
Distant objects (such as the Sun) send almost parallel rays, so a converging lens focuses them at F: this is a simple way to **measure focal length**.

callouts.p: Focus an image of a distant window onto a screen; the lens to screen distance is approximately the focal length.

core.p: A diverging lens refracts parallel rays away from the principal axis so they spread out. If you trace the spreading rays backwards with dashed lines, they all appear to come from a single point on the same side as the incoming light: the virtual principal focus.
bullets: Parallel rays are **spread out (diverge)** after the lens.
The rays **appear to come from** the principal focus on the **same side** as the incoming light.
The focus is **virtual**: no light actually passes through it.
Show the trace-back lines as **dashed** lines because they are not real rays.
The ray along the principal axis passes straight through.

callouts.p: Draw construction lines to a virtual focus or virtual image dashed. Solid lines mean light really travels there.

core.h: Power of a lens, focal length and shape
core.p: The power of a lens describes how strongly it bends (converges or diverges) light. A more curved lens has surfaces at steeper angles to incoming rays, so it refracts them more and brings them to a focus closer to the lens. That is why a more curved lens has a shorter focal length and a greater power.
bullets: **More curved** (fatter) lens: refracts light **more**, **shorter focal length**, **more powerful**.
**Less curved** (flatter) lens: refracts light **less**, **longer focal length**, **less powerful**.
Power and focal length are **inversely related**: the shorter the focal length, the greater the power.
For the same focal length, a lens made from a material that refracts light more can be made **thinner**.
A diverging lens also becomes more powerful the more curved it is, spreading light more strongly.

callouts.p: More curved lens, greater refraction, shorter focal length, more powerful lens.

core.p: An image is where light from an object appears to come from after passing through a lens. Whether an image is real or virtual depends on whether the rays actually meet there.
bullets: A **real image** forms where light rays **actually meet**; it **can be projected on a screen**.
Real images formed by a single lens are always **inverted** (upside down) and on the **opposite side** of the lens from the object.
A **virtual image** forms where rays only **appear to come from**; it **cannot be projected on a screen**.
Virtual images from a single lens are **upright** and on the **same side** as the object.
Converging lenses can make **real or virtual** images; diverging lenses only make **virtual** images.

head: Property
Real image
Virtual image
rows: Converging lens (object inside F) or any diverging lens

callouts.p: An image formed where light rays actually meet, which can be projected onto a screen.
An image formed where light rays only appear to come from, which cannot be projected onto a screen.

core.h: Drawing ray diagrams for a converging lens
core.p: To find an image you only need two rays from the top of the object; where they meet (or appear to meet) is the top of the image. A third ray is a useful check. Always draw with a ruler and mark F on both sides.
bullets: **Ray 1**: from the top of the object **parallel to the principal axis**, then refracted **through F** on the far side.
**Ray 2**: from the top of the object **straight through the centre** of the lens, undeviated.
**Ray 3** (check): from the top of the object **through F on the near side**, then leaving the lens **parallel** to the axis.
Where the rays **cross** is the top of the image; draw the image from the axis to that point.
If the rays **diverge** after the lens, extend them **backwards with dashed lines**; where they meet is a virtual image.
Draw the refraction as a single bend at the **centre line** of the lens to keep diagrams simple.

callouts.p: Examiners award marks for correct parallel-then-through-F and through-centre rays, arrows on rays, and the image drawn where they cross.

core.h: Converging lens: image depends on object position
core.p: As an object moves closer to a converging lens, the image moves further away and gets bigger, until at F no image forms at all. Inside F the image switches from real to virtual. Learn this table: it underpins cameras, projectors and magnifying glasses.
bullets: Far away (beyond 2F): **real, inverted, diminished**, between F and 2F. Used in **cameras** and the eye.
At 2F: **real, inverted, same size**, at 2F on the other side.
Between F and 2F: **real, inverted, magnified**, beyond 2F. Used in **projectors**.
At F: refracted rays are **parallel**, so **no image** forms (or 'image at infinity').
Inside F (between F and lens): **virtual, upright, magnified**, on the same side as the object. Used as a **magnifying glass**.

callouts.p: Object outside F gives a real image; object inside F gives a virtual image.

core.h: The magnifying glass: a virtual image
core.p: When an object is closer to a converging lens than the principal focus, the lens cannot bend the rays enough to make them meet. They leave the lens diverging. Your eye traces them back to a point behind the object, where you see a larger, upright, virtual image.
bullets: Object must be **between the lens and F**.
Rays **diverge** after the lens, so trace them **back** with **dashed lines**.
Image is **virtual, upright and magnified**, on the **same side** as the object.
You must look **through the lens** from the other side to see the image; it cannot be put on a screen.
A more powerful (more curved, shorter focal length) lens gives greater magnification.

callouts.p: Saying the magnifying glass image is real is a very common error. It is virtual, because the rays only appear to come from it.

core.h: Ray diagrams for a diverging lens
core.p: A diverging lens always produces the same kind of image wherever the object is placed. The rays always spread out after the lens, so they never meet; the image is always where they appear to come from.
bullets: **Ray 1**: from the top of the object **parallel to the axis**, then refracted **away from the axis** as if it came from **F on the object side**; draw the trace-back to F dashed.
**Ray 2**: from the top of the object **through the centre** of the lens, undeviated.
The image is where the dashed line from Ray 1 meets Ray 2 (on the object side).
Image is always **virtual, upright, diminished**, and **between F and the lens** on the same side as the object.
Diverging lenses are used in **glasses for short-sighted people** and in some door peepholes to give a wide view.

callouts.p: Always virtual, upright and diminished, on the same side of the lens as the object.

core.p: Exam questions often ask you to describe an image. A complete description has three or four parts and examiners give a mark for each.
bullets: **Nature**: real or virtual.
**Orientation**: upright or inverted.
**Size**: magnified, diminished or same size compared with the object.
**Position**: which side of the lens and roughly where (for example between F and 2F).
Use your ray diagram to read the answers: compare the image arrow with the object arrow.

callouts.p: Write 'real/virtual, upright/inverted, magnified/diminished' every time; it is easy to forget one property under pressure.

core.p: Each lens application uses one row of the image table. Knowing why each device needs a particular object position shows grade 9 understanding.
bullets: **Camera**: converging lens; distant object beyond 2F gives a **real, inverted, diminished** image on the sensor.
**Human eye**: the converging cornea and lens form a real, inverted, diminished image on the **retina**.
**Projector**: slide placed between F and 2F gives a **real, inverted, magnified** image on a screen; the slide is put in upside down so the picture is the right way up.
**Magnifying glass**: object inside F gives a **virtual, upright, magnified** image.
**Long sight** is corrected with **converging** lenses; **short sight** is corrected with **diverging** lenses.

analogy.p: A converging lens is like a funnel for light: a wide stream of parallel rays is squeezed down to a single spot, the principal focus, and the steeper the funnel's sides (a more curved lens), the shorter the distance to that spot, so the funnel is more powerful. A diverging lens is like a garden sprinkler head: a straight stream goes in and spreads out, and if you trace the spray back it seems to come from a single point behind the head, just like a virtual focus. Where it breaks down: a funnel physically pushes water together, whereas a lens bends light by changing its speed (refraction); and the analogy says nothing about images, which depend on where the object is placed relative to F.

terms.d: A shaped piece of transparent material that changes the direction of light by refraction.
A convex lens, thicker in the middle, that brings parallel rays together at a principal focus.
A concave lens, thinner in the middle, that spreads parallel rays out so they appear to come from a principal focus.
The line through the centre of the lens at 90 degrees to it.
The centre of the lens; rays through it are not deviated.
The point where rays parallel to the principal axis meet (converging lens) or appear to come from (diverging lens).
The distance from the centre of the lens to the principal focus.
How strongly a lens converges or diverges light; a shorter focal length means a more powerful lens.
An image formed where rays actually meet; it can be projected on a screen.
An image formed where rays only appear to come from; it cannot be projected on a screen.
Upside down compared with the object.
The same way up as the object.
Larger than the object.
Smaller than the object.
A scale drawing using straight-line rays to show how a lens forms an image.
A converging lens used with the object inside the focal length to give a virtual, upright, magnified image.

mistakes.w: A more curved lens has a longer focal length.
mistakes.r: A more curved lens refracts more, so it has a shorter focal length and is more powerful.

mistakes.w: Focal length is the distance from the lens to the image.
mistakes.r: Focal length is the distance from the centre of the lens to the principal focus.

mistakes.w: A magnifying glass forms a real image.
mistakes.r: It forms a virtual, upright, magnified image that cannot be projected on a screen.

mistakes.w: A diverging lens can form a real image if the object is close.
mistakes.r: A diverging lens always forms a virtual, upright, diminished image.

mistakes.w: Lenses work by reflecting light.
mistakes.r: Lenses work by refraction, changing the direction of light as it changes speed.

mistakes.w: The ray through the centre of the lens bends towards F.
mistakes.r: The ray through the centre of the lens passes straight through undeviated.

mistakes.w: Drawing trace-back lines to a virtual image as solid lines.
mistakes.r: Construction lines to a virtual image or virtual focus are dashed because no light travels along them.

mistakes.w: A real image is upright.
mistakes.r: A real image formed by a single converging lens is always inverted.

mistakes.w: Rays parallel to the axis leave a diverging lens and meet at F on the far side.
mistakes.r: They spread out and appear to come from F on the same side as the incoming light.

exam.q: Define the focal length of a lens.
model: The distance from the centre of the lens to the principal focus.
exam.tip: Say 'centre of the lens' and 'principal focus'.

exam.q: State the difference between a real image and a virtual image.
model: A real image is formed where rays actually meet / can be projected on a screen
A virtual image is where rays only appear to come from / cannot be projected on a screen
exam.tip: Give one clear property of each.

exam.q: Two converging lenses have the same diameter. Lens A is more curved than lens B. Explain which lens is more powerful.
model: Lens A
A more curved lens refracts light more
so it has a shorter focal length (and greater power)
exam.tip: Chain: curvature, refraction, focal length, power.

exam.q: Describe the effect of a diverging lens on rays of light travelling parallel to the principal axis.
model: The rays are spread out / diverge
they appear to come from the principal focus on the same side as the incident light
exam.tip: Mention 'appear to come from' for the second mark.

exam.q: Describe how you could measure the focal length of a converging lens.
model: Use the lens to focus light from a distant object (e.g. a window) onto a screen
Move the lens until the image is sharp
Measure the distance from the centre of the lens to the screen: this is approximately the focal length
exam.tip: Distant object means the rays are nearly parallel.

exam.q: Complete a ray diagram for an object placed at 2F from a converging lens and describe the image formed.
model: Ray parallel to the axis refracted through F on the far side
Ray through the centre of the lens undeviated
Image at 2F on the opposite side
Image is real, inverted and same size
exam.tip: Arrows on rays and a clearly marked image arrow are needed.

exam.q: An object is placed 3 cm from a converging lens of focal length 5 cm. State three properties of the image.
model: Virtual
Upright
Magnified (on the same side as the object)
exam.tip: 3 cm is inside the focal length: that tells you it is a magnifying glass arrangement.

exam.q: Explain why the image formed by a diverging lens can never be projected onto a screen.
model: The rays always diverge after passing through the lens and never meet
so the image is only where they appear to come from, which is a virtual image
exam.tip: Link diverging rays to virtual image.

exam.q: A projector uses a converging lens to produce a large image of a slide on a screen. State where the slide must be placed and explain why it is put in upside down.
model: Between F and 2F
The image is real and magnified
A real image is inverted, so the slide is inserted upside down to give an upright picture on the screen
exam.tip: Match the device to the row of the image table.

exam.q: Use ray diagrams to explain how a converging lens can form both real and virtual images, and compare these with the image formed by a diverging lens.
model: Converging lens: ray parallel to axis refracted through F; ray through centre undeviated
Object beyond F: rays converge and actually meet on the far side, giving a real, inverted image that can be projected
Object inside F: rays diverge after the lens; traced back (dashed) they appear to meet on the object side
This gives a virtual, upright, magnified image (magnifying glass)
Diverging lens: parallel ray refracted so it appears to come from F on the object side; ray through centre undeviated
Rays always diverge so the image is always virtual, upright and diminished, between F and the lens
exam.tip: A logical structure: converging real, converging virtual, then diverging. Describe the rays, not just the result.

worked.q: An object 2 cm tall is placed 6 cm from a converging lens of focal length 4 cm. Using a scale ray diagram, describe the position, size and nature of the image.
steps: Draw the principal axis and lens; mark F at 4 cm and 2F at 8 cm on both sides.
Draw the object arrow 2 cm tall, 6 cm from the lens: it is between F and 2F.
Ray 1: from the top of the object parallel to the axis, then through F on the far side.
Ray 2: from the top of the object straight through the centre of the lens.
The rays cross 12 cm from the lens on the far side, 4 cm below the axis.
Image height 4 cm compared with object 2 cm: twice the size.
worked.ans: Real, inverted, magnified (4 cm tall, twice the object size), 12 cm from the lens on the opposite side, beyond 2F.

worked.q: Lens X has a focal length of 10 cm and lens Y has a focal length of 25 cm. Both are made of the same glass. Which is more powerful, and which is more curved?
steps: Power increases as focal length decreases.
Lens X has the shorter focal length (10 cm compared with 25 cm), so it is more powerful.
A shorter focal length means the lens refracts light more strongly.
For the same material, stronger refraction requires more curved surfaces.
worked.ans: Lens X is more powerful and more curved.

worked.q: A stamp is held 2 cm behind a converging lens of focal length 8 cm. Explain why the student sees a larger upright image, and why she cannot catch it on a screen.
steps: The stamp is between the lens and F (2 cm is less than 8 cm).
Rays from the stamp are refracted but still diverge after leaving the lens.
The eye traces the diverging rays back in straight lines to a point further away on the stamp's side.
There the rays appear to come from a larger, upright image.
Because the rays never actually meet at the image, it is virtual and cannot be projected on a screen.
worked.ans: The image is virtual, upright and magnified; it is virtual because the rays only appear to come from it, so it cannot be formed on a screen.
